formation.title: The Rise of the Songhai Empire
formation.text:
The Niger River bends through the heart of our land like a great artery of civilization. From Gao to Timbuktu, from the salt mines of Taghaza to the gold fields of Wangara, a new empire rises to claim dominion over the greatest trade routes in Africa.

But what shall define this empire? Shall we follow the path of Sunni Ali: the warrior who never lost a battle, who struck from river and land with devastating speed, who bent the Niger to his will through sheer military force? Or shall we walk the road of Askia Muhammad: the pilgrim-emperor who transformed a military conquest into a civilization of law, scholarship, and faith, making Timbuktu the intellectual capital of the Islamic world?

The river stretches before us. The choice is ours.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the riders of the Niger. Let our enemies tremble.

modifiers.name: Lord of the River
modifiers.text: In the tradition of Sunni Ali, the Songhai Empire wages war with unmatched speed along the Niger, striking from river and land simultaneously.

options.text: We shall build a throne of knowledge and justice.

modifiers.name: The Scholar's Throne
modifiers.text: Following Askia Muhammad's vision, the Songhai Empire becomes a beacon of Islamic learning and just governance across the Sahel.

advances.name: Children of the River
advances.text: The Songhai people have lived along the Niger since time immemorial, drawing life from its floods and fish.

advances.name: Songhai Noble Cavalry
advances.text: The mounted warriors of Songhai, clad in iron breastplates beneath their battle tunics, are the backbone of imperial power.

advances.name: The Hi-Koy's Fleet
advances.text: The river admiral commands the war canoes of the Niger. His crews are the Sorko, the fishing people of the river. Their boats carry grain and men behind an army on the march, so that it can stand far from its depots.

advances.name: Faith of the Sahel
advances.text: Islam arrived along the trade routes, embraced first by merchants and rulers, gradually transforming Songhai spiritual life.

advances.name: Foundation of Gao
advances.text: Gao stands at the great bend of the Niger, the ancestral seat of Songhai power and gateway to the Sahara.

advances.name: Floodplain Farming
advances.text: The annual floods of the Niger deposit rich silt across the plains, sustaining the agriculture that feeds the empire.

advances.name: Trans-Saharan Caravans
advances.text: Camel caravans cross the desert bearing gold, salt, ivory, and cloth: the lifeblood of Sahelian commerce.

advances.name: The Conquests of Sunni Ali
advances.text: Sunni Ali the Great was never defeated in battle. Through riverine and cavalry warfare, he forged the Songhai Empire.

advances.name: Command of the Hi-Koy
advances.text: The Hi-Koy commands over a thousand vessels from the port of Gao. His canoes carry the grain of the Askia's armies along the Niger and stock the depots from which they march.

advances.name: The Jewel of the Sahel
advances.text: The conquest of Timbuktu in 1468 brought the greatest trading city in West Africa under Songhai control.

advances.name: Saharan Mounted Archers
advances.text: Mounted archers drawn from nomadic traditions serve as screens and raiders, harassing enemies before the heavy cavalry strikes.

advances.name: The Askia Dynasty
advances.text: Askia Muhammad's seizure of the throne transformed Songhai from a military state into an Islamic empire of law and administration.

advances.name: Gold and Salt Monopoly
advances.text: Gold flows north; salt flows south. The Songhai sit astride both streams, taxing the most valuable exchange in Africa.

advances.name: The Hajj of Askia Muhammad
advances.text: Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496 established Songhai as a legitimate Islamic power in the eyes of the wider Muslim world.

event.title: The Pilgrimage of the Askia
event.text:
In 1496, Askia Muhammad departed Gao with a retinue of five hundred cavalry and one thousand foot soldiers, bearing three hundred thousand gold pieces for charitable distribution along the route. His hajj to Mecca was no mere act of personal devotion; it was a diplomatic masterstroke. In the Holy Cities, he was received by the Abbasid Caliph in Cairo, who invested him with the title Caliph of the Lands of Takrur, granting the Songhai throne religious legitimacy that no predecessor had possessed.

He returned with scholars, architects, and merchants. He brought the jurist al-Maghili from Tlemcen to serve as his chief advisor. He carried the idea that Timbuktu could become not merely a trading post but a seat of learning to rival Cairo and Baghdad. The pilgrimage transformed a military empire into a cultural one.

options.text: The world now knows the glory of Songhai.

modifiers.name: Pilgrim of the Two Holy Cities
modifiers.text: The Emperor's pilgrimage to Mecca has elevated Songhai's standing among the Muslim world, bringing scholars and merchants to our courts.

advances.name: The Five Viceroyalties
advances.text: The empire is divided into five great provinces, each governed by a viceroy who maintains order while allowing local autonomy.

advances.name: The University of Sankore
advances.text: Twenty-five thousand students study in Timbuktu's Sankore quarter, making it one of the great centers of learning in the Islamic world.

event.title: The University of Sankore
event.text:
In the Sankore quarter of Timbuktu, under the shadow of the great mud-brick mosque, some twenty-five thousand students gather to study under scholars who have mastered theology, law, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and history. The Sankore is not one institution but a constellation of private scholars, each with their own students and libraries, united by a shared commitment to the Maliki school of Islamic jurisprudence.

Students must arrive fluent in Arabic and with the entire Qur'an committed to memory. The degrees they earn, comparable to the ijazah of Cairo's al-Azhar, are recognized across the Muslim world. Timbuktu's libraries house hundreds of thousands of manuscripts, the greatest concentration of written knowledge in sub-Saharan Africa.

options.text: Knowledge is the true gold of Timbuktu.

advances.name: Courts of the Qadi
advances.text: Islamic magistrates administer justice according to Sharia law in every major city, bringing order and predictability to governance.

advances.name: The Emperor's Standard
advances.text: Standardized weights and measures, enforced by trade inspectors in every market, have made Songhai commerce the most trusted in the Sahel.

event.title: The Emperor's Standard
event.text:
Askia Muhammad did what no Sahelian ruler before him had attempted: he imposed a system of standardized weights and measures across the empire's markets. Trade inspectors, the muhtasib, were stationed in every major market center from Timbuktu to Gao to Djenne, empowered to verify scales, enforce fair dealing, and punish fraud.

The result was a commercial revolution. Merchants from Cairo to Fez to Venice could trade with confidence in Songhai markets, knowing that a measure of gold in Timbuktu weighed the same as a measure of gold in Gao. The empire's reputation for fair dealing drew caravans from across the Sahara like water to a well.

options.text: Fair trade builds stronger empires than conquest.

advances.name: The Prosperity of Djenne
advances.text: Djenne, city of a thousand scholars and the greatest mosque in the Sudan, flourishes as a center of commerce and culture.

advances.name: The Imperial Guard
advances.text: A professional standing army forms the iron core of Songhai military power, loyal to the Askia dynasty alone.

advances.name: Lords of the Desert
advances.text: Camel-mounted warriors patrol the Saharan frontier, protecting caravans and projecting imperial authority into the deep desert.

advances.name: The Manuscripts of Timbuktu
advances.text: Hundreds of thousands of manuscripts fill the libraries of Timbuktu, preserving knowledge of astronomy, medicine, history, and law.

advances.name: The Koi System
advances.text: Regional military commanders, the Koi, maintain standing forces across the empire, ensuring rapid response to any threat.

advances.name: The Muhtasib
advances.text: Trade inspectors enforce fair dealing in every market, verifying weights, punishing fraud, and collecting imperial customs.

advances.name: The Thunder Answered
advances.text: The Moroccan invasion demonstrated the devastating power of firearms. The empire must adapt or perish.

event.title: Thunder from the North
event.text:
In 1591, Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco sent an army of four thousand men under the Spanish eunuch Judar Pasha across the Sahara: a journey of four months through waterless desert. They brought with them eight English cannons and thousands of arquebus-armed infantry. At the Battle of Tondibi, the Songhai army of forty thousand faced this smaller but devastatingly armed force.

The Songhai commander Askia Ishaq II ordered a stampede of one thousand cattle to break the Moroccan lines, but the thunderclap of gunfire panicked the herd back into Songhai ranks. The battle lasted barely two hours. Gao, Timbuktu, and Djenne all fell within months.

The age of the great Saharan empires was ending. But empires die slowly in the desert. The question now is how we face the future.

options.text: Fortify the cities. We will not yield a single grain of sand.

modifiers.name: Defenders of the Niger
modifiers.text: Against the thunder of foreign cannons, the Songhai stand firm in defense of their homeland and the cities of the Niger.

options.text: Fall back into the hinterland: the desert is our fortress.

modifiers.name: The Sahel Retreats into the Sand
modifiers.text: Let the invaders take the empty cities. The Songhai know the desert, the river, and the paths between. We will endure.

advances.name: Wealth of the Herds
advances.text: Vast herds of cattle, goats, and horses sustain the Sahel's pastoral economy and provide cavalry mounts for the imperial army.

advances.name: The Maliki School
advances.text: The Maliki school of Islamic law, brought by scholars from North Africa, provides a unifying legal framework across the empire's diverse peoples.

advances.name: Empire of Many Peoples
advances.text: Songhai, Mandinka, Tuareg, Fulani: the empire governs a mosaic of peoples through flexible administration and shared Islamic faith.

advances.name: Resilience of the Sahel
advances.text: Empires rise and fall, but the people of the Sahel endure. The Songhai legacy survives in successor states and cultural memory.

advances.name: Niger Commerce
advances.text: The Niger remains the highway of West African trade, carrying goods and ideas between forest and desert.

advances.name: Fortifications of the Sahel
advances.text: Mud-brick walls and defensive compounds protect Sahelian cities from raiders and invaders alike.

advances.name: Authority of the Askia
advances.text: The central authority of the Askia tightens its grip over provincial governors, ensuring imperial unity.

advances.name: Soldiers of the Empire
advances.text: Slave soldiers, personally loyal to the emperor rather than any clan or family, form a reliable core of professional troops.

advances.name: Keepers of Knowledge
advances.text: Through oral tradition and carefully preserved manuscripts, Songhai scholars keep alive the learning of centuries.

advances.name: Songhai Revival
advances.text: A new generation reclaims the legacy of the Askia dynasty, kindling the dream of a restored Songhai civilization.

advances.name: Modern Sahel Agriculture
advances.text: New techniques transform the floodplains and savanna into more productive farmland, feeding a growing population.

advances.name: Modern Saharan Trade
advances.text: The ancient trade routes find new life as modern infrastructure connects the Sahel to global markets.

advances.name: Modern Songhai Army
advances.text: A reformed and modernized military ensures the Songhai Empire can defend its sovereignty in a changing world.

advances.name: Education for All
advances.text: Building on Timbuktu's scholarly tradition, new schools bring literacy and learning to all corners of the empire.

advances.name: The Dream of Restoration
advances.text: From Gao to Timbuktu, the vision of a restored Songhai Empire unites the people of the Niger bend.

destiny.name: Destiny of the Songhai
destiny.text: The Songhai Empire has risen. Now it must choose its path: conquest or enlightenment.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of Songhai
event.text: The Songhai Empire stands at a crossroads. The Niger bends before us, the desert stretches behind, and the future lies in our hands. Whether we choose the sword or the pen, the empire shall endure.

destiny.name: Saharan Salt Roads
destiny.text: Seize the salt mines of the Sahara and crush the Mossi kingdoms to secure the empire's southern frontier. Control Taghaza and Ouagadougou.

conditions.text: Chose Lord of the River
Own Taghaza, or a subject owns it
Own Ouagadougou, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000

event.title: The Salt Roads Are Ours
event.text: The great salt caravans that cross the Sahara now move under Songhai protection. From Taghaza to the markets of the Sahel, every bar of salt enriches our treasury. The Mossi kingdoms have been humbled, and the southern frontier is secure.

options.text: Salt is the wealth of the desert.

destiny.name: Conquest of Hausaland
destiny.text: March east into Hausaland. Keep river ports at three landings to carry the army, and take Kano, Katsina, and the Bornu capital of Ngazargamu to dominate the central Sahel.

conditions.text: Own Kano, or a subject owns it
Own Katsina, or a subject owns it
Own Ngazargamu, or a subject owns it
At least 3 of our locations have a Niger River Port

event.title: The Fall of Hausaland
event.text:
The walled cities of Hausaland have fallen to our armies. Kano, that great center of Saharan commerce, lies under Songhai authority. Katsina's dye pits and Bornu's Lake Chad frontier are ours. But how shall we govern these conquered peoples?

We may extract tribute and leave local rulers in place, enriching the treasury while preserving stability. Or we may integrate these lands fully into the imperial system, accepting their peoples as our own, though this strains our administrative capacity.

options.text: Extract tribute from the conquered cities.

modifiers.name: Tribute of Hausaland
modifiers.text: The conquered cities of Hausaland pay tribute to the Askia, filling the treasury while local rulers maintain order under Songhai oversight.

modifiers.name: Peoples of the Empire
modifiers.text: The peoples of Hausaland are welcomed into the imperial fold, their cultures accepted as part of the Songhai mosaic.

destiny.name: Hegemony of the Sahel
destiny.text: Push south into the gold fields of Asante and take Sokoto, and hold half of Hausaland directly or through subject kings. No power in West Africa may rival the Songhai Empire.

conditions.text: Own Kumasi, or a subject owns it
Own Bono Manso, or a subject owns it
Own Sokoto, or a subject owns it
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least half of the locations in the North Hausa area and in the South Hausa area
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Lords of the Sahel
event.text:
From the gold fields of Asante to the salt mines of Taghaza, from the Niger bend to the borders of Bornu, no power in West Africa can rival the Songhai Empire. Our armies have achieved what Sunni Ali dreamed: total dominion over the Sahel.

Shall we rule as the Iron Askia, projecting unstoppable military power across the region? Or shall we embrace the empire of dust: mastering the terrain itself, making the desert and savanna our greatest fortress?

options.text: We are the Iron Askia: none shall stand against us.

modifiers.name: The Iron Askia
modifiers.text: The Songhai army strikes with the speed and precision of Sunni Ali reborn, overwhelming enemies before they can mount a defense.

options.text: The desert is our fortress and our weapon.

modifiers.name: Empire of Dust
modifiers.text: The Sahel itself fights for the Songhai. Invaders founder in the desert while our armies move with ease across familiar terrain.

destiny.name: Masters of the Gold Trade
destiny.text: Control the sources of gold at Begho and ensure gold flows through Songhai markets. Wealth is the foundation of civilization.

event.title: Gold Flows Through Songhai
event.text: The gold of the south now passes through Songhai hands. At Begho and in our markets, the precious metal is weighed, taxed, and sent north across the Sahara. Merchants from across the Muslim world come to trade in our cities, drawn by the reliability of our weights and the fairness of our courts.

destiny.name: City of Knowledge
destiny.text: Build up Timbuktu to 15 development and found a library there for the manuscripts of its scholars, so that it can serve as the intellectual capital of Africa.

conditions.text: We own Timbuktu and its development is at least 15
We own Timbuktu and it has a Library
Prestige at least 50

event.title: The Flowering of Timbuktu
event.text:
Timbuktu has become what Askia Muhammad always envisioned: a city where scholarship and commerce are inseparable, where the wealth of the gold trade funds libraries and madrasas, where students come from across the Muslim world to study under Songhai masters.

Shall we deepen the scholarly networks, attracting more learned men to our courts even at the cost of military readiness? Or shall we cultivate merchant-scholars who combine trade acumen with intellectual refinement, though some diplomats may find our commercial focus uncouth?

options.text: Scholarship above all: knowledge is eternal.

modifiers.name: Network of Scholars
modifiers.text: A web of correspondence connects Songhai scholars to the great minds of the Islamic world, accelerating the spread of knowledge.

modifiers.name: Merchant-Scholars of the Niger
modifiers.text: The learned merchants of Timbuktu combine commercial acumen with intellectual depth, driving prosperity across the Niger basin.

destiny.name: Beacon of Africa
destiny.text: Build up Gao, the capital of the Askias, to 18 development, keep libraries in three of our cities, and make the Songhai Empire the most prestigious power in Africa.

Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75

event.title: The Beacon of Africa
event.text:
The Songhai Empire has achieved what no sub-Saharan power has done before. Timbuktu rivals Cairo as a center of Islamic learning. Gao has grown into the greatest city the Sahel has seen. Libraries in three of our cities keep the manuscripts that once existed only in fragile copies.

Shall we embrace a golden age of culture, making Timbuktu the undisputed intellectual capital of the Islamic world? Or shall we build a universal empire, binding diverse peoples together through shared faith and mutual obligation?

options.text: Let Timbuktu shine as the jewel of Islam.

modifiers.name: Golden Age of Timbuktu
modifiers.text: Timbuktu enters its greatest era: a city of a hundred thousand manuscripts, where scholarship, art, and faith illuminate the Sahel.

options.text: We shall build an empire of many peoples and one faith.

modifiers.name: The Universal Empire
modifiers.text: The Songhai Empire transcends tribal boundaries, binding Songhai, Mandinka, Tuareg, and Hausa into a single community of faith and obligation.

units.name: Songhai Noble Cavalry
units.text: Elite mounted warriors of the Songhai nobility, clad in iron breastplates beneath their battle tunics, who charge the enemy with devastating force.

units.name: Hi-Koy Marines
units.text: River warriors who fight from the great war canoes of the Niger fleet, equally deadly in amphibious assault and close combat.

units.name: Songhai Mounted Archers
units.text: Light cavalry archers from the Saharan tradition, used for scouting, screening, and harassing enemy formations before the main assault.

units.name: Songhai Imperial Guard
units.text: The professional soldiers of the Askia dynasty, heavily equipped and fanatically loyal to the emperor.

units.name: Songhai War Canoe
units.text: Large dugout war canoes carrying armed marines, the backbone of the Niger River fleet commanded by the Hi-Koy.

units.name: Saharan Camel Corps
units.text: Camel-mounted warriors who patrol the Saharan frontier, protecting caravans and striking deep into the desert.

units.name: Songhai Jihad Infantry
units.text: Religiously motivated warriors fighting in defense of the Islamic state, their fervor compensating for the empire's lack of firearms.

units.name: Sahel Musketeer
units.text: Infantry armed with acquired firearms, adapting the lessons of Tondibi to ensure the empire is never again caught without gunpowder weapons.

buildings.name: Sankore Madrasa
buildings.text: A center of Islamic learning modeled on the great Sankore mosque in Timbuktu, where scholars teach theology, law, medicine, and astronomy.

buildings.name: Saharan Caravanserai
buildings.text: A fortified rest stop along the trans-Saharan trade routes, providing shelter, water, and markets for traveling merchants.

buildings.name: Niger River Port
buildings.text: A landing on the river, where canoes are built and repaired and where grain, salt and soldiers are loaded for the journey along the Niger.

buildings.name: Qadi Court
buildings.text: An Islamic judicial court where the Qadi administers justice according to Sharia law, bringing order and legitimacy to imperial governance.

buildings.name: Imperial Granary
buildings.text: A mud-brick storehouse that collects and preserves the bounty of the Niger floodplains, insuring against famine and feeding the empire's cities.

buildings.name: Gold Market
buildings.text: A trading house where the gold of Wangara is weighed, assayed, and exchanged for the salt of Taghaza and the cloth of the Mediterranean.

buildings.name: Mosque of Djenne
buildings.text: A monumental mud-brick mosque in the tradition of Djenne's great architecture, inspiring devotion and cultural pride.

buildings.name: Muhtasib Office
buildings.text: The headquarters of the imperial trade inspector, who enforces standardized weights, fair dealing, and market regulations.

buildings.name: Slave Soldier Barracks
buildings.text: Quarters for slave soldiers personally loyal to the emperor, forming a reliable professional military force independent of clan loyalties.

buildings.name: Assay House
buildings.text: A house beside the market where gold dust is weighed against the imperial standard, refined, and worked into pieces of known weight. It stands only where a market is held.

buildings.name: House of Copyists
buildings.text: A house of paid copyists in the manner of Timbuktu, where each finished book carries the name of the man who copied it and of the scholar who checked it.

buildings.name: Sahel Stud
buildings.text: Pastures where the small, hardy horses of the Niger bend are bred on millet for the cavalry and the caravans. It is found where horses are already raised in the market's lands.

children.text: Horses is produced in the market

buildings.name: Mud-Brick Town Wall
buildings.text: A wall of sun-dried brick with gates and watch platforms, renewed after every rainy season, like the wall of Djenne that held Sunni Ali's army for years. A town can raise it; a city builds stronger walls.

buildings.name: Imperial War Camp
buildings.text: A fortified staging ground where the Askia marshals his armies, stores plunder, and plans the next campaign of conquest.

buildings.name: House of Wisdom
buildings.text: A grand institution of learning where scholars translate, copy, and compose works of theology, science, and philosophy in the tradition of Baghdad's Bayt al-Hikma.

list.name: Office of the Hi-Koy
list.text: The admiralty of the Niger river fleet: the most distinctive Songhai office and one without precedent in Mali. The Hi-Koy commanded a flotilla of armoured war-canoes that carried the Askia's troops up and down the inland delta from Gao to Jenne, transported salt and grain to the imperial markets, and enforced toll collection at the river crossings. The position coexisted uneasily with the cavalry nobility: the river fleet was built around fishing castes (the Sorko, Bozo, and Somono) whom the cavalry despised but on whom imperial logistics depended.

list.name: Askia Provincial Farmas
list.text: Askia Muhammad's reform of 1493 onward divided the empire into appointed governorships: Kurmina-Fari over the west, Dendi-Fari over the south, Bana-Farma over the east, plus Hari-Farma of the lakes, Sao-Farma of the woodlands, Fari-Mondio of the Dirma plains, and Yufu-Mondio of the rivers. Where Sunni Ali had ruled through tributary chiefs, the Askia appointed loyalists (often relatives, often former slave-officers) whose tenure was at the throne's pleasure. The farma system was the spine of Songhai centralisation and the feature most resented by the displaced Sonni-era aristocracy.

list.name: Mori-Koyra Inquisitor Court
list.text: On his return from the hajj of 1496-97, Askia Muhammad consulted the North African scholar Muhammad al-Maghili, whose Replies to the Questions of the Amir of Songhai prescribed a rigorous purge of mixed Islamic practice and the office of an inquisitor (mori-koyra, the great scholar) empowered to pursue apostasy, syncretism with Bori and Hauka spirit cults, and noble misuse of the law. The institution gave the imperial throne a religious-judicial reach into the countryside that the nobility could not block, but it inflamed the still-pagan rural majority who saw their ancestral practices criminalised.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Tarikh Chronicle Scribes
list.text: The literate Soninke, Sanhaja, and Songhai scribal class who staffed the Askias' chancery and from whose ranks came the chroniclers of the Tarikh as-Sudan, finished by Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di of Timbuktu in 1655, and the Tarikh al-Fattash, begun under Askia Muhammad by the Kati family and continued for over a century. Unlike the oral djeli tradition of Manden, this was a documentary bureaucracy: appointment letters, tax registers, jurisprudential fatwas, and the genealogies that legitimised the Askia line. The chroniclers preserved Songhai institutional memory, often subtly against the throne whenever they thought the throne had erred.

list.name: Rumde Standing Corps
list.text: The Askia's standing army of war-captives and conscripted servile labour (rumde, arbi) distinct from the seasonal levies of the noble cavalry. Recruited through campaigns along the Niger and across the Mossi country, equipped from imperial armouries at Gao, and quartered year-round, the rumde gave the Askias an instrument independent of and a counterweight to the Sonni-era cavalry aristocracy. Their year-round availability made possible the extended Mande, Mossi, Hausa, and Saharan campaigns that defined the imperial period; their cost forced the inflation of the slave-tribute that weighed on the peasantry.

list.name: Tondi-Farma Royal Estates
list.text: The imperial domain lands of the Niger bend: rice fields at Dendi, cattle pastures along the lakes, millet plantations on the floodplain, all worked by zanj war-captives and administered by a Tondi-Farma (master of the fields) reporting directly to the Askia. The royal estates fed the standing army, supplied the Gao court, and gave the throne an income independent of the kharaj tax that had to be negotiated with provincial chiefs. They also tied a substantial unfree population to the crown, a fact which after Tondibi in 1591 became the seedbed of revolt.
